passage: Last year my photo page looked perfect: the debate trophy, the beach trip, the new haircut. I spent twenty minutes on every caption. People left hearts under everything, and I, Yamini, still ate lunch pretending to text so nobody would notice I had nobody to talk to. I was scared that if anyone saw how often I doubted myself, they'd leave. Then in March, Vaibhav from my bus stop asked why a girl with such a perfect page never looked happy in person. I almost said, "I'm fine." Instead I said, "I don't know who I am when I'm not performing." He didn't laugh. He said he felt the same about his gym videos. We talk at the bus stop most mornings now. It's only one person. It's more than all those hearts.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav ask Yamini in March?
qa.a: He asked why a girl with such a perfect page never looked happy in person.

qa.q: Why did Yamini pretend to text at lunch?
qa.a: She was afraid people would notice she had nobody to talk to, and worried that showing her doubts would make them leave.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Yamini, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Choosing to say "I don't know who I am when I'm not performing" instead of "I'm fine." One honest answer let a real friendship begin.

qa.q: What might Vaibhav have gained from Yamini's honest reply?
qa.a: It gave him room to admit he felt the same about his gym videos, so he didn't have to feel alone either.

grounding: A teenager hides doubts behind a polished online self, feels alone among many followers, and one real disclosure starts to change that.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Class 10. Parveen.
Imran (15) came in to "ask about streams" and spent ten minutes on marks. Classmates see him as the funny one, and his short videos get big numbers. Near the end, looking at the floor, he said, "Everyone knows me and nobody knows me." He told me he deletes any post where he looks tired or unsure. I thanked him for telling me, said many students feel this and it isn't a weakness, and asked if there was one person he'd trust with one small true thing. He named his cousin Faiz. Plan: he will tell Faiz one honest thing this week. I'll check in with him at lunch on Wednesday, and we meet again on Friday.

qa.q: What did Imran say he deletes?
qa.a: Any post where he looks tired or unsure.

qa.q: What does Imran looking at the floor while saying "Everyone knows me and nobody knows me" suggest?
qa.a: He feels lonely behind his funny image and is nervous about admitting it, as if afraid of being judged.

qa.q: Why was asking Imran to share one small true thing with Faiz a good step?
qa.a: It keeps the risk small, so he can test whether honesty brings rejection or closeness, with the counsellor checking in along the way.

qa.q: How might Faiz be affected if Imran shares something honest?
qa.a: Faiz may feel trusted and closer to Imran, and might open up in return 🙂

grounding: A teenager who shows a polished, funny self feels unknown and alone, and a counsellor helps him take a first small step toward real disclosure.

passage:
Thursday, 10:40 pm
The class group was full of Samir's birthday pics tonight. I'm in six of them, laughing. Nobody would guess I spent half the party in the washroom because I felt like a fake.
I keep a version of me for them: chill, good at football, never stressed. The real one is scared of failing the maths re-test and thinks nobody would stay if they saw him.
But on the walk home Samir asked, "Bro, you okay? You went missing." And I said... actually, no. Told him about the re-test. He said he failed chemistry last term and hid it too!!
Didn't expect that. Feel lighter. Also weird. Going to sleep.
Kunal

qa.q: Where did Kunal spend half of Samir's party?
qa.a: In the washroom.

qa.q: Why did Kunal feel like a fake at the party?
qa.a: He was hiding his fear about the maths re-test behind a chill, never-stressed version of himself, and worried nobody would stay if they saw the real him.

qa.q: What choice on the walk home changed things for Kunal?
qa.a: When Samir asked, Kunal told the truth about the re-test instead of saying he was fine, and found he wasn't alone.

qa.q: How might Samir have felt when Kunal went missing at the party?
qa.a: Samir noticed and seems to have been worried, and may have felt relieved to share the hidden chemistry result too.

grounding: A teenager who keeps a polished image feels fake and alone among friends until one honest disclosure brings unexpected closeness.

passage:

Jagdish: discipline 😎
Preeti: teach me
Jagdish: wake up at 5, no excuses
Preeti: ok but real question. you seemed off at the canteen today
Jagdish: nah just tired
Preeti: ok
Jagdish: actually
Jagdish: can I tell you something without it going anywhere
Preeti: of course
Jagdish: I haven't played that guitar in months. I post old videos. and I'm so scared about boards I can't sleep
Jagdish: everyone thinks I've got it together. if they knew they'd think I'm a fraud

Jagdish: really?
Preeti: really. study together tomorrow? no posting
Jagdish: yeah. thanks. first time I've said any of this to anyone

qa.q: What does Jagdish admit about the guitar videos?
qa.a: Jagdish hasn't played that guitar in months and posts old videos.

qa.q: What is Jagdish afraid will happen if people learn the truth?
qa.a: Jagdish fears everyone would see a fraud instead of someone who has it all together.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the chat, and why did it matter?
qa.a: When Jagdish typed 'actually' and told the truth; that small disclosure let Preeti admit being scared too and offer to study together.

qa.q: What might it be like for Preeti to hear Jagdish's confession?
qa.a: Preeti may feel trusted, and relieved to say the same fear out loud, since Preeti also hides it by simply not posting.

grounding: A teenager who shows a polished self online admits in a late chat to fear and faking, and one real disclosure begins to ease feeling alone.

passage:
Everyone at the tuition centre near the Jorhat tea estate knew Bhupen, fifteen: the boy who did impressions of the sir, always had a joke and never seemed to study. On the bus home the back seat crowded around him.
He never mentioned that his mother had gone to work in Bengaluru in March, or that he cooked rice for his little brother every night and fell asleep over his books. When the others talked about their mothers' cooking, he cracked a joke and looked out of the window.
One evening the bus broke down and only Alka was left at the stand with him. "You're funny," she said, "but you always look tired." He almost laughed it off. Then he told her about the rice, and his mother's voice on the phone. Alka didn't say much. "My father works away too." They waited in silence, and it felt less lonely than the crowded back seat.

qa.q: Where had Bhupen's mother gone to work in March?
qa.a: She had gone to work in Bengaluru.

qa.q: Why did Bhupen crack a joke and look out of the window when others talked about their mothers' cooking?
qa.a: He was hiding how much he missed his mother, afraid that showing it would change how the others saw him.

qa.q: At the bus stand, what did Bhupen choose instead of laughing it off, and what did it change?
qa.a: He told Alka about cooking rice and his mother's calls, and that honest moment felt less lonely than the crowded back seat.

qa.q: What might it mean to Alka that Bhupen trusted her with this?
qa.a: Alka might feel trusted and understood, since her own father works away too.

grounding: A popular, joking teenager hides his loneliness at home, feels alone in the crowd, and begins to change it through one honest disclosure.
